nodes.claim: Any partition of the plane into regions of equal area has perimeter at least that of the regular hexagonal tiling (2D).
nodes.note: v0.4 (2026-11-24): scope: the 2D cross-section perimeter only. The theorem is about a partition of the plane into regions of equal area; it says nothing about cell depth, the cell base, volume or wax mass. Reference: Hales, Discrete Comput Geom 25:1-22 (2001), journal reference as given on the arXiv record. What the v0.3 note said about the repository record is kept in status_history and on the root node P_HEX_CELL.

nodes.claim: The 3D bee cell (three-rhombus base) is not surface-minimizing; two hexagons + two rhombi is more economical, saving <0.35% of the opening area.
nodes.note: With non-zero wall thickness the three-rhombus base may be closer to optimum (Weaire & Phelan, as reported in Apidologie 2022). Optimality in 3D is regime-dependent on wall thickness.

nodes.claim: Wall thickness: zero (idealized) vs real non-uniform beeswax walls.
Cells are built circular; visco-elastic wax heated by workers flows near triple junctions; surface-energy minimization straightens walls into rounded hexagons.
nodes.note: Three accounts preserved, not reconciled: (a) surface-tension wax flow (Karihaloo 2013); (b) thermal expansion and stress above yield under a temperature gradient, without melting (Talukdar & Dutta, SN Appl Sci 2019); (c) workers iteratively equalising angular space at junctions, self-organised (npj/Nature 2026). Divergence is retained as data. | v0.3 (2026-11-24): (d) direct construction: bees shape wax with antennae, mandibles and legs, wax 33.6–37.6 °C, no liquid equilibrium (Bauer & Bienefeld, Naturwissenschaften 100:45–49, 2013). Earlier liquid-equilibrium account: Pirk et al. 2004. Irregular building under constraint: Smith, Napp & Petersen, PNAS 118:e2103605118, 2021. Label correction: the v0.2 source cited as 'Nature 2026' is Gallo, Bridges, Woodgate & Chittka, npj Entomology, published 2026-10-06 https://www.nature.com/articles/s44434-026-00004-2.

nodes.claim: Wax flows visco-elastically at about 45 °C at the triple junction.
nodes.note: v0.3 (2026-11-24): CONTESTED. Bauer & Bienefeld 2013 (infrared and thermographic video) measured wax at 33.6–37.6 °C during hexagonal-cell construction, below the ~40 °C they take as needed for liquid equilibrium; Karihaloo 2013 gives about 45 °C. Both kept; not reconciled. The original claim text is unchanged.

nodes.claim: Beeswax melts at 62–64 °C (upper regime bound: comb structure fails).
Brood nest regulated at 33–36 °C; capped brood 34.8–35.9 °C across ambient 13–41 °C.
Derived operating regime for hexagon formation: local wax ~45 °C, nest ~33–36 °C, below melt 62–64 °C.
nodes.note: Lower bound 45 °C is 'about'; treat as CONDITIONAL until a source gives a range. | v0.3 (2026-11-24): the 45 °C lower bound comes from C_FLOW_T, now CONTESTED; the regime is CONDITIONAL on which account holds. Bauer & Bienefeld's 33.6–37.6 °C would fall below this bound.

nodes.claim: Beeswax composition: monoesters 35–45%, hydrocarbons 12–16%, free fatty acids 12–14%; hydrocarbons probably from oenocytes.
Secreted as liquid by four pairs of wax glands on young workers; glands largest ~day 12, decline after day 18; ~1 million scales per kg.
Wax is synthesised from sugar: ~8 kg honey consumed per kg wax.

value.deviation: sources span 6.66–8.80 (Whitcomb 1946, via Wikipedia) to 8–15 (FAO T0104E)

nodes.claim: Heat for wax working and brood comes from worker thoracic muscle metabolism fuelled by nectar sugar; ~40% of the colony's annual energy intake goes to brood-nest heating.
Nectar sugars originate from sucrose loaded from phloem, produced by photosynthesis.
Total solar irradiance at 1 AU: 1360.8 ± 0.5 W/m² (2008 solar minimum).
nodes.note: GAP: no repository entity represents incoming solar radiation. SOLAR_WIND is a plasma flow.

nodes.claim: Open, far-from-equilibrium systems maintain ordered structure only through continuous energy/matter exchange and disappear if it ceases (dissipative structures).
nodes.note: Energy conservation is assumed as the accounting law for the chain; no repository equation reference exists for it.

nodes.claim: Flowering plants supplying nectar.
nodes.note: Which repository plant entities stand for nectar sources is an owner decision. v0.2 (2026-11-24): split into D4_MANUKA and D4_WILDFLOWER in the environment differential.

nodes.claim: Workers heat the wax with their bodies during comb building.
Atmospheric attenuation leaves ≈1000 W/m² maximum normal irradiance at sea level on a clear day; clear-sky noon values range ≈700–1300 W/m² with latitude, altitude and time of year.
Theoretical maximum conversion of solar energy to biomass: 4.6% (C3) / 6% (C4) at 30 °C and 380 ppm CO2; 9.4% / 12.3% of photosynthetically active radiation. Field values are much lower.

value.deviation: upper bound, not a typical value

nodes.claim: Honeybees use solar azimuth and the sky polarization pattern (produced by atmospheric scattering of sunlight) as a compass; the sun's movement is compensated by an internal circadian clock.
nodes.note: Role is information, not energy: the dependency is on the geometry of sunlight, not its power. Repo dependency string 'time_of_day' binds here (PROPOSED).

nodes.claim: Scattering of sunlight in the atmosphere produces a regular pattern of E-vectors tangential to concentric circles around the sun.
nodes.note: Named as stated by source; the scattering theory itself (e.g., Rayleigh) is not cited here -> UNCHECKED beyond the source's statement.

nodes.claim: Mānuka (Leptospermum scoparium): green, photosynthetic nectaries; nectar dominated by fructose and glucose with small, variable sucrose and dihydroxyacetone (DHA), usually <2% each.
nodes.note: GAP: no repository entity for mānuka.

nodes.claim: Nectary photosynthesis contributes a measurable share of mānuka nectar sugars (¹³CO₂ label appears in nectar sugars incl. DHA); the rest is phloem import. Nectar DHA derives from triose-phosphate (DHAP) pools.
Multifloral forage: many species; honey composition reflects the botanical mix and is more variable than monofloral honey.

In honey, nectar-derived DHA converts non-enzymatically to methylglyoxal (MGO): overall first-order, studied 4–37 °C. Fresh comb honey DHA 1192–5099 mg/kg vs MGO 139–491 mg/kg; DHA falls and MGO rises in storage. Commercial mānuka: mean DHA:MGO ≈2:1, MGO 70–700 mg/kg.
nodes.note: Control: DHA added to clover honey produced MGO at mānuka-like levels (Adams 2009). The chemistry is set by the nectar input, not the bee.

nodes.claim: The Fejes Tóth cell's surface-area economy can be improved beyond the FT gain to 0.50% by increasing the tilt of the hexagonal faces by 2.8°.

value.unit: fraction of cell surface area saved

nodes.note: v0.3 (2026-11-24): Dauter & Jaskolski, Acta Cryst. A 2025. Mathematical; an optimum, not a measurement of bees. Lead from Kimi (2026-11-25), who called it a review; it presents new analysis.

nodes.claim: Natural combs of Apis cerana cerana and Apis mellifera ligustica contain no more than 18% Fejes Tóth cells on average; bees can build them but mostly build three-rhombus cells. Measured dihedral angle at the cell bottom: 108.70° ± 0.16° (n = 238 cells), against a theoretical 120°.

value.deviation: ± 0.16 as reported; statistic type and species of this sample not checked; other samples 109.60 ± 0.44, 108.70 ± 0.20, 111.10 ± 0.26

nodes.note: v0.3 (2026-11-24): Yang et al., Apidologie 53:6, 2022. The measured gap between the D0 optimum and the built artifact. It is a sourced quantity, not noise.

nodes.claim: The three-rhombus (444) cell base that honeybees build is not the most economical in wax. Fejes Tóth (1964) found a base of two hexagons and two rhombi (6464) whose gain over the 444 base is less than 0.35% of the hexagonal cross-section area; increasing the tilt of its hexagonal faces by 2.8° raises the gain to 0.50% over the 444 base.
source: Fejes Tóth, L. (1964). Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 70, 468–481 (as listed in the references of the article above; not opened)

value.unit: % surface-area economy over the tri-rhombic 444 base

status_history.note: node added in v0.4. It joins G3D_FEJES and G3D_DAUTER, which stay as they are.

nodes.note: v0.4 (2026-11-24): status per source read. Not opened: the 1964 paper (ams.org did not answer from this machine); the owner's order gives it as Bull AMS 70(4), the article lists volume 70, pages 468–481; the issue number is not confirmed here. cycles.name: circle→hexagon transition
cycles.period_text: ≈6 s fully heated; ≈36 s partially heated
cycles.note: A relaxation, not a repeat. Recorded as a transient phase inside the comb-building cycle; whether it counts as a cycle in its own right is an owner call.

cycles.name: daily activity (circadian)
cycles.period_text: ≈24 h endogenous; free-runs slightly off 24 h in constant conditions; entrains to light–dark cycles; period ≈24 h at both 23 °C and 31 °C (temperature-compensated)
cycles.note: v0.2 (2026-11-24): sourced. The same clock drives time memory and sun-compass compensation (Beier & Lindauer 1970 as reported). External driver: the light–dark cycle.

cycles.name: wax-gland age window
cycles.period_text: begins <1 wk, peaks ≈2 wk (≈day 12), declines after day 18
cycles.context: worker life stage; swarm regime overrides (all ages build)

cycles.name: colony annual cycle
cycles.period_text: 1 year (winter cluster vs summer energy partition)

cycles.name: mānuka flowering window
cycles.period_text: usual 10–12 weeks; 4 weeks in a short season (MPI 2018); 6–12 weeks, often less, Sept–March, <6 weeks in Taranaki (Landcare)
cycles.note: period_s set to 8 weeks as a midpoint for ordering only; the record keeps the range.

cycles.name: mānuka flower nectar stages

cycles.note: Duration in days not given by these sources.
